imo-2026-01.title: Monovariants, then a Euclidean-algorithm invariant
imo-2026-01.body:
**(a)** Note $\gcd(m,n)\cdot\frac{\operatorname{lcm}(m,n)}{\gcd(m,n)}=\operatorname{lcm}(m,n)=\frac{mn}{\gcd(m,n)}$. Consider a move on $m,n>1$ with $g=\gcd(m,n)$.
- If $g=1$, the two numbers become $1$ and $mn$: the number of $1$'s on the board goes up by one, and the product of all numbers is unchanged.
- If $g>1$, the product of all numbers is divided by $g$, so it strictly decreases.

A $1$ is never chosen, so the number of $1$'s never decreases and is at most $2026$; hence there are at most $2026$ moves of the first kind. The product of the numbers never increases and is a positive integer, so there are finitely many moves of the second kind. So the process stops after finitely many moves, i.e. at some point fewer than two numbers exceed $1$.

On the other hand, a move never makes both new numbers equal to $1$: if $g=1$ the second number is $mn>1$. So every move takes two numbers $>1$ and leaves at least one number $>1$, and since initially there are numbers $>1$, there is always at least one. Hence at the end exactly one number $M$ is greater than $1$.

**(b)** Fix a prime $p$. For the numbers $t_1,\dots,t_{2026}$ on the board consider
$$D_p=\gcd\bigl(\nu_p(t_1),\dots,\nu_p(t_{2026})\bigr)$$
(the gcd of nonnegative integers, with $\gcd(0,\dots,0)=0$). Let a move act on $m,n$ with $\nu_p(m)=x\le\nu_p(n)=y$. Then $\nu_p(\gcd(m,n))=x$ and $\nu_p\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{lcm}(m,n)}{\gcd(m,n)}\right)=y-x$. Since $\gcd(x,y-x)=\gcd(x,y)$ and the other numbers are unchanged, $D_p$ is invariant.

At the end the board holds $M$ and $2025$ ones, so $D_p=\nu_p(M)$. Therefore, if the initial numbers are $a_1,\dots,a_{2026}$,
$$\nu_p(M)=\gcd\bigl(\nu_p(a_1),\dots,\nu_p(a_{2026})\bigr)\quad\text{for every prime }p,$$
which depends only on the initial numbers. As $M$ is determined by all its exponents $\nu_p(M)$, it does not depend on the choices of Confucius. ∎

imo-2026-02.title: Three cyclic quadrilaterals and power of a point
imo-2026-02.body:
Throughout, $\measuredangle(\ell_1,\ell_2)$ is the directed angle between lines (mod $180^\circ$), and products like $PQ\cdot PR$ of collinear points are signed (positive iff $Q,R$ are on the same side of $P$). For a circle $\omega$ and a line through $P$ meeting $\omega$ at $Q,R$ (with $Q=R$ for a tangent), $PQ\cdot PR$ is the power of $P$; conversely, if two different lines through $P$ contain $Q,R$ and $S,U$ with $PQ\cdot PR=PS\cdot PU\neq0$, then $Q,R,S,U$ are concyclic (if $Q=R$: the circle through $Q,S,U$ is tangent to $PQ$ at $Q$).

**Step 0: the conditions as directed angles.** Orient $ABC$ counterclockwise. For an undirected angle, $\measuredangle(QP,QR)=+\angle PQR$ iff triangle $PQR$ is oriented clockwise. Using the hypotheses on positions:
- $(K,B,A)$ has the orientation of $(C,B,A)$ ($K$, $C$ on the same side of $AB$) and $(A,C,L)$ that of $(A,C,B)$; both clockwise.
- $(L,B,K)$ has the orientation of $(L,B,A)$ ($K$ inside $ABL$), which is that of $(C,B,A)$; $(L,N,C)$ has that of $(B,N,C)$ ($L$ inside $BNC$), i.e. of $(B,A,C)$; both clockwise.
- $(L,C,K)$ has that of $(A,C,K)$ ($L$ inside $AKC$), i.e. of $(A,C,B)$; $(B,M,K)$ has that of $(B,M,C)$ ($K$ inside $BMC$), i.e. of $(B,A,C)$; both clockwise.

So the three equalities hold for directed angles:
$$\measuredangle(BK,BA)=\measuredangle(CA,CL),\quad \measuredangle(BL,BK)=\measuredangle(NL,NC),\quad \measuredangle(CL,CK)=\measuredangle(MB,MK).$$

**Step 1: three circles.** Let $X=BK\cap AC$ and $Y=CL\cap AB$; as $K,L$ are inside the triangle, $X$ and $Y$ are interior points of segments $AC$ and $AB$.
- The first equality reads $\measuredangle(BX,BY)=\measuredangle(CX,CY)$, so $B,C,X,Y$ are concyclic. Power of $A$: $AY\cdot AB=AX\cdot AC$, hence
$$AY\cdot AM=AX\cdot AN=\tfrac12AX\cdot AC.\tag{1}$$
- Let $\omega_C$ be the circle $CMK$ (not collinear, as $K$ is inside $BMC$). It meets $AB$ at $M$ and a second point $Y^*$ ($Y^*=M$ if tangent; $Y^*\ne C$). By inscribed angles, $\measuredangle(CY^*,CK)=\measuredangle(AB,MK)=\measuredangle(MB,MK)=\measuredangle(CL,CK)$, so $CY^*=CL$ and $Y^*=Y$. Thus $Y\in\omega_C$.
- Similarly let $\omega_B$ be the circle $BNL$; its second point $X^*$ on $AC$ satisfies $\measuredangle(BX^*,BL)=\measuredangle(AC,NL)=\measuredangle(NC,NL)=\measuredangle(BK,BL)$, so $X^*=X$ and $X\in\omega_B$.

**Step 2: midpoints.** Let $C'$ be the second intersection of line $AC$ with $\omega_C$ and $B'$ that of line $AB$ with $\omega_B$. The power of $A$ and (1) give $AC\cdot AC'=AM\cdot AY=\frac12AC\cdot AX$, so $AC'=\frac12AX$: $C'$ is the midpoint of $AX$. Likewise $AB\cdot AB'=AN\cdot AX=\frac12AB\cdot AY$, so $B'$ is the midpoint of $AY$.

Let $E$ and $F$ be the midpoints of $BY$ and $CX$. Note $A,E,F$ are not collinear ($E\in AB$, $F\in AC$, both $\neq A$).

**Step 3: $A,E,F,K,L$ are concyclic.** Let $K'$ be the second intersection of line $BX$ with $\omega_C$. Put coordinates on line $AC$ with $A=0$, $X=x$, $C=c$; then $C'=\frac x2$, $F=\frac{x+c}2$ and
$$XC\cdot XC'=(c-x)\left(-\tfrac x2\right)=(-x)\cdot\tfrac{c-x}2=XA\cdot XF.$$
By the power of $X$ with respect to $\omega_C$, $XK\cdot XK'=XC\cdot XC'=XA\cdot XF\neq0$, so $A,F,K,K'$ are concyclic. Since $M$ and $E$ are the midpoints of $BA$ and $BY$, the power of $B$ gives
$$BK\cdot BK'=BM\cdot BY=\tfrac12BA\cdot BY=BA\cdot BE,$$
so $A,E,K,K'$ are concyclic. The point $A$ is not on line $BX$, so if $K'\neq K$ both circles are the circle through the non-collinear points $A,K,K'$; if $K'=K$ both are the unique circle through $A$ tangent to $BX$ at $K$. Either way $K$ lies on the circle $(AEF)$.

In the same way, with $L'$ the second intersection of line $CY$ with $\omega_B$: the power of $Y$ gives $YL\cdot YL'=YB\cdot YB'=YA\cdot YE$ (on line $AB$: $YB\cdot YB'=(b-y)(-\frac y2)=(-y)\frac{b-y}2$), and, as $N,F$ are the midpoints of $CA,CX$, the power of $C$ gives $CL\cdot CL'=CN\cdot CX=\frac12CA\cdot CX=CA\cdot CF$. Hence $L$ also lies on $(AEF)$.

Since $A,K,L$ are distinct points of the circle $(AEF)$, it is the circumcircle of $AKL$; so $O$ is its centre. Let $\rho$ be its radius.

**Step 4: equal powers.** Line $AB$ meets $(AEF)$ at $A$ and $E$; with $A=0$, $B=b$, $Y=y$ on this line, $M=\frac b2$ and $E=\frac{b+y}2$, so
$$\operatorname{pow}(M)=MA\cdot ME=\left(-\tfrac b2\right)\cdot\tfrac y2=-\tfrac14\,AB\cdot AY.$$
Similarly $\operatorname{pow}(N)=NA\cdot NF=-\frac14\,AC\cdot AX$. By (1), $AB\cdot AY=AC\cdot AX$, so $OM^2-\rho^2=ON^2-\rho^2$, i.e. $OM=ON$. ∎

imo-2026-03.title: Greedy claiming, a powers-of-two division and pigeonhole
imo-2026-03.body:
**Claiming phase.** If the pieces are $x_1\ge x_2\ge\dots\ge x_m$, then under best play Liu gets exactly $x_1+x_3+x_5+\cdots$. Indeed, if Liu always takes the largest remaining piece, at his $j$-th turn only $2j-2$ pieces are gone, so he gets at least $x_{2j-1}$; if Xiang always takes the largest piece, at his $j$-th turn only $2j-1$ pieces are gone, so he gets at least $x_{2j}$, and Liu gets at most $1-(x_2+x_4+\cdots)$. Put
$$G=x_1-x_2+x_3-x_4+\cdots,$$
so Liu's result is $\frac{1+G}2$. Note that if the pieces consist of equal pairs plus one extra piece $r$, then $G=r$ (the pairs cancel in the sorted alternating sum), and $G=0$ if all pieces are paired. Our claim $c=\frac{2^n}{2^{n+1}-1}$ is equivalent to: Liu can force $G\ge\frac1{2^{n+1}-1}$, and Xiang can always force $G\le\frac1{2^{n+1}-1}$.

Call the pieces created by Liu's marks alone **segments**.

**Liu's strategy.** Scale the stick to length $2^{n+1}-1$ and let Liu cut it into segments of lengths $1,2,4,\dots,2^n$ ($n$ marks). Xiang makes at most $n$ cuts, so there are at most $2n+1$ pieces; pad the sorted list with zeros to $x_1\ge\dots\ge x_{2n+1}\ge0$.

*Claim.* For $k=0,1,\dots,n$: $x_2+x_4+\dots+x_{2k}\le 2^{n-1}+2^{n-2}+\dots+2^{n-k}$.

*Proof.* Induction on $k$; $k=0$ is trivial. Suppose it holds for $k-1$ but fails for $k$. Subtracting, $x_{2k}>2^{n-k}$, hence $x_1,\dots,x_{2k}$ all exceed $2^{n-k}$. Each piece lies inside a segment, so these $2k$ pieces lie inside the $k$ segments $2^{n-k+1},\dots,2^n$, giving $x_1+\dots+x_{2k}\le2^{n-k+1}+\dots+2^n$. As $x_{2i}\le x_{2i-1}$,
$$x_2+x_4+\dots+x_{2k}\le\tfrac12(x_1+\dots+x_{2k})\le 2^{n-k}+\dots+2^{n-1},$$
a contradiction. $\square$

With $k=n$, Xiang gets at most $2^n-1$, so Liu gets at least $2^n$ out of $2^{n+1}-1$, i.e. $\frac{2^n}{2^{n+1}-1}$ of the stick.

**Xiang's strategy.** If Liu marks fewer than $n$ points, there are at most $n$ segments; Xiang bisects each one, all pieces are paired, $G=0$ and Liu gets only $\frac12$. So assume Liu marks exactly $n$ points, giving $n+1$ segments. For a set $S$ of segments let $\Sigma(S)$ be its total length.

*Lemma.* If $S,T$ are disjoint sets of segments, not both empty, with $\Sigma(S)\ge\Sigma(T)$, then Xiang can force $G\le\Sigma(S)-\Sigma(T)$.

*Proof.* Lay the segments of $S$ end to end on an interval $[0,\Sigma(S)]$ (the "$S$-line") and those of $T$ on $[0,\Sigma(T)]$ (the "$T$-line"); these are just bookkeeping pictures of the real segments. Xiang cuts:
1. at every position in $(0,\Sigma(T))$ that is a segment endpoint on exactly one of the two lines, on the other line; and at position $\Sigma(T)$ on the $S$-line if it is interior to an $S$-segment;
2. if $\Sigma(S)>\Sigma(T)$: the $S$-line part $[\Sigma(T),\Sigma(S)]$ is divided into pieces by $S$-segment endpoints; he leaves the first of these pieces alone and bisects every other one (each is a whole $S$-segment);
3. he bisects every segment in neither $S$ nor $T$.

All these cut points are interior points of segments and distinct. On $[0,\Sigma(T)]$ the two lines are now cut at the same positions, so their pieces pair up exactly; the bisected pieces pair up; the only unpaired piece is the first piece of $[\Sigma(T),\Sigma(S)]$, of length at most $\Sigma(S)-\Sigma(T)$ (none if $\Sigma(S)=\Sigma(T)$). So $G\le\Sigma(S)-\Sigma(T)$.

Count of cuts: let $|S|=s$, $|T|=t$, and $u=n+1-s-t$ others; let $\alpha$ be the number of interior $S$-endpoints in $(0,\Sigma(T))$. Step 1 uses at most $t+\alpha$ cuts ($t-1$ interior $T$-endpoints plus $\Sigma(T)$, and the $\alpha$ $S$-endpoints); step 2 uses at most $(s-1)-\alpha$ (the interior $S$-endpoints beyond $\Sigma(T)$); step 3 uses $u$. Total $\le s+t+u-1=n$. $\square$

*Pigeonhole.* The $2^{n+1}$ subsets of the $n+1$ segments have sums in $[0,1]$; sorting them, the $2^{n+1}-1$ consecutive gaps add up to $1$, so two different subsets $S_1\ne S_2$ satisfy $0\le\Sigma(S_1)-\Sigma(S_2)\le\frac1{2^{n+1}-1}$. Removing their common segments gives disjoint $S,T$, not both empty, with the same difference. By the lemma Xiang forces $G\le\frac1{2^{n+1}-1}$, so Liu gets at most $\frac12\left(1+\frac1{2^{n+1}-1}\right)=\frac{2^n}{2^{n+1}-1}$.

**Answer: $c=\dfrac{2^n}{2^{n+1}-1}$.** ∎

imo-2026-04.title: Multiples of $\theta$: reach one, or avoid them all
imo-2026-04.body:
Call an angle **unsafe** if it is an integer multiple of $\theta$, and **safe** otherwise. The multiples of $\theta$ form an additive group $Z=\{k\theta:k\in\mathbb Z\}$, so the sum or difference of a number in $Z$ and a number not in $Z$ is not in $Z$.

**Mulan wins if $\theta=\frac{180^\circ}n$, $n\ge2$.**

*Lemma.* If $\mathcal T$ has an angle $k\theta$ ($k\ge1$ an integer), Mulan can win. By induction on $k$: for $k=1$ the game is over. For $k\ge2$ she cuts from that vertex $V$ to a point of the opposite side so that the angle at $V$ is split into $\theta$ and $(k-1)\theta$; whichever triangle Shan-Yu keeps has an angle $\theta$ or $(k-1)\theta$ at $V$.

*Strategy.* First Mulan cuts along the altitude from the vertex with the largest angle; since the other two angles are acute, its foot is an interior point of the opposite side, and both pieces are right triangles. If $n=2$ this angle is $90^\circ=\theta$ and she has won. If $n\ge3$, the kept triangle is $ABC$ with $\angle A=90^\circ$ and, say, $\angle B=\beta\le45^\circ$. Some multiple $k\theta$ ($k\ge1$) lies in $(45^\circ,90^\circ]$: for $n=3$ take $k=1$; for $n\ge4$, $\theta\le45^\circ$ is at most the length of this interval. As $D$ runs along $BC$ from $B$ to $C$, the exterior angle $\angle ADC=\beta+\angle BAD$ increases continuously from $\beta$ to $\beta+90^\circ$; since $\beta\le45^\circ<k\theta\le90^\circ<\beta+90^\circ$, there is an interior point $D$ with $\angle ADC=k\theta$. Mulan cuts along $AD$. The two triangles have angles $\angle ADC=k\theta$ and $\angle ADB=180^\circ-k\theta=(n-k)\theta$ at $D$, with $k\ge1$ and $n-k\ge1$, so by the lemma she wins.

**Shan-Yu survives if $\theta\neq\frac{180^\circ}n$.** Then $180^\circ\notin Z$ (as $180^\circ=k\theta$ would force $k\ge2$ and $\theta=\frac{180^\circ}k$). Call a triangle safe if all its angles are safe.

Shan-Yu starts with a safe triangle: $Z\cap(0^\circ,180^\circ)$ is finite, so he can choose angles $\alpha_1,\alpha_2$ avoiding it with $\alpha_1+\alpha_2<180^\circ$ and $180^\circ-\alpha_1-\alpha_2$ avoiding it as well.

*Claim.* If a safe triangle $ABC$ is cut along $AD$ ($D$ inside $BC$), at least one of $ABD$, $ADC$ is safe. Indeed,
$$\angle ADC=\angle B+\angle BAD=180^\circ-\angle ADB,\qquad \angle DAC=\angle A-\angle BAD=\angle ADB-\angle C.$$
Suppose $ABD$ is unsafe; as $\angle B$ is safe, $\angle BAD\in Z$ or $\angle ADB\in Z$.
- If $\angle BAD\in Z$: $\angle ADC=\angle B+\angle BAD\notin Z$ and $\angle DAC=\angle A-\angle BAD\notin Z$.
- If $\angle ADB\in Z$: $\angle ADC=180^\circ-\angle ADB\notin Z$ and $\angle DAC=\angle ADB-\angle C\notin Z$.

Together with $\angle C\notin Z$, triangle $ADC$ is safe. $\square$

So Shan-Yu always keeps a safe triangle; no triangle ever has an angle $\theta$, and Mulan never wins.

**Answer: Mulan can force a win exactly when $\theta=\frac{180^\circ}n$ for some integer $n\ge2$.** ∎

imo-2026-05.title: Orbits are arithmetic progressions
imo-2026-05.body:
**These work.** If $f(x)=x+c$ with $c\ge0$, then $\frac{f(x)+y}2=\frac{x+(y+c)}2=\frac{x+f(y)}2$, and the inequalities are QM $\ge$ AM $\ge$ GM for the positive numbers $x$ and $f(y)$. ($c\ge0$ is needed for $f$ to be positive near $0$.)

**Only these work.** Let $P(x,y)$ be the left inequality and $Q(x,y)$ the right one.

*Step 1: orbits are arithmetic.* $P(f(t),t)$ gives $f(t)\ge\frac{f(f(t))+t}2$ and $Q(f(t),t)$ gives $\frac{f(f(t))+t}2\ge f(t)$. So $f(f(t))=2f(t)-t$ for all $t$. Applying this to $t,f(t),f^2(t),\dots$ shows that $t,f(t),f^2(t),\dots$ is an arithmetic progression: $f^k(t)=t+k\,d(t)$ with $d(t)=f(t)-t$. All terms are positive, so $d(t)\ge0$; and $d(f^k(t))=d(t)$.

*Step 2: positive differences are equal.* Let $d(x)=A>0$, $d(y)=B>0$. For integers $m,n\ge0$ put $X=x+mA$ and $W=y+(n+1)B$; then $f(X)=X+A$ and $f(y+nB)=W$. $Q(X,\,y+nB)$ reads
$$\frac{X+A+W-B}{2}\ge\sqrt{XW}\iff\left(\sqrt X-\sqrt W\right)^2\ge B-A .$$
Suppose $B>A$ and let $\varepsilon=\sqrt{B-A}>0$. Then $|\sqrt{x+mA}-\sqrt{y+(n+1)B}|\ge\varepsilon$ for all $m,n\ge0$. But $\sqrt{x+(m+1)A}-\sqrt{x+mA}=\frac{A}{\sqrt{x+(m+1)A}+\sqrt{x+mA}}\to0$, so for $m\ge m_0$ these gaps are less than $\varepsilon$; choosing $n$ with $\sqrt{y+(n+1)B}\ge\sqrt{x+m_0A}$, the number $\sqrt{y+(n+1)B}$ lies within $\varepsilon$ of some $\sqrt{x+mA}$, a contradiction. So $B\le A$, and by symmetry $A=B$.

Hence either $f(x)=x$ for all $x$ (that is $c=0$), or there is $D>0$ with $f(x)\in\{x,\ x+D\}$ for every $x$. Assume the latter and let $S_1=\{x: f(x)=x+D\}\neq\varnothing$, $S_0=\{y:f(y)=y\}$.

*Step 3: $S_0$ is empty.* Let $x\in S_1$, $y\in S_0$ (so $x\neq y$).
- If $x>y$: $P(x,y)$ gives $\frac{x+D+y}2\le\sqrt{\frac{x^2+y^2}2}<x$, so $x-y>D$.
- If $x<y$: $Q(y,x)$ gives $\sqrt{y(x+D)}\le\frac{y+x}2<y$, so $x+D<y$.

So $|x-y|>D$ whenever $x\in S_1$, $y\in S_0$. If some $y\in S_0$ existed, take $x\in S_1$ and split the segment from $x$ to $y$ into $N$ equal parts of length $\le D$ with points $x=z_0,z_1,\dots,z_N=y$. Each $z_i$ is in $S_0$ or $S_1$, $z_0\in S_1$ and $z_N\in S_0$, so some consecutive $z_i\in S_1$, $z_{i+1}\in S_0$ are at distance $\le D$, a contradiction. Hence $f(x)=x+D$ for all $x$.

**Answer: $f(x)=x+c$ for any constant $c\ge0$.** ∎

imo-2026-06.title: Only small primes matter
imo-2026-06.body:
Let $\mathcal A=\{a_1,a_2,\dots\}$; the sequence is strictly increasing, and any two of its terms have a common factor.

**Description of $\mathcal A$.** For an integer $x\ge a_1$:
$$x\in\mathcal A\iff \gcd(x,a)>1\ \text{for all } a\in\mathcal A \text{ with } a<x \iff \gcd(x,a)>1\ \text{for all } a\in\mathcal A.\tag{1}$$
If $x=a_1$ the first condition is empty, and if $x=a_{n+1}$ it is the definition; and the second holds because terms pairwise share a factor. If $x\notin\mathcal A$ satisfies the first condition, pick $n$ with $a_n<x<a_{n+1}$; then $x$ is a candidate for $a_{n+1}$ smaller than $a_{n+1}$, a contradiction. The second condition implies the first.

**Redundant terms.** Write $\operatorname{rad}(z)$ for the product of the distinct primes dividing $z$. Call $a_n$ *minimal* if there is no $m<n$ with $\operatorname{rad}(a_m)\mid\operatorname{rad}(a_n)$. For every $a_n$ there is a minimal $a_m$ with $m\le n$ and $\operatorname{rad}(a_m)\mid\operatorname{rad}(a_n)$ (go down repeatedly). If $\gcd(x,a_m)>1$ then some prime divides $x$ and $a_m$, hence also $a_n$. Therefore in both conditions of (1) we may restrict $a$ to minimal terms:
$$x\in\mathcal A\iff\gcd(x,a)>1\ \text{for all minimal } a\in\mathcal A \text{ with } a<x \iff\gcd(x,a)>1\ \text{for all minimal } a\in\mathcal A.\tag{2}$$

**Key claim: no minimal term has a prime factor $p>a_1^2$.** Strong induction on $n$. The prime factors of $a_1$ are $\le a_1<a_1^2$. Let $n\ge2$ and suppose $a_n=pc$ with a prime $p>a_1^2$. Take a prime $q\mid\gcd(a_1,a_n)$; then $q\le a_1<p$, so $q\mid c$. Since $a_n\ge p>a_1^2\ge q\,a_1$, the interval $[a_1,a_n)$ has ratio $>q$, so some number $z=q^jc$ ($j\ge0$) lies in $[a_1,a_n)$: if $c\ge a_1$ take $z=c<a_n$, otherwise the first $q^jc\ge a_1$ is $<qa_1<a_n$.

We check $z\in\mathcal A$ via the first form of (2). Let $a_i<z$ be minimal. Then $i<n$, so by the induction hypothesis $p\nmid a_i$. Some prime $r$ divides both $a_n$ and $a_i$; $r\neq p$, so $r\mid c\mid z$. Hence $\gcd(z,a_i)>1$, and as $z\ge a_1$, $z\in\mathcal A$; say $z=a_m$, with $m<n$ because $z<a_n$. Every prime factor of $z$ ($q$ or a factor of $c$) divides $a_n$, so $\operatorname{rad}(a_m)\mid\operatorname{rad}(a_n)$ and $a_n$ is not minimal. This proves the claim.

**Periodicity.** Let $\mathcal P$ be the (finite, nonempty) set of primes $\le a_1^2$ and $L=\prod_{p\in\mathcal P}p$. For a minimal $a$, all prime factors lie in $\mathcal P$, so $\gcd(x,a)>1$ iff some $p\in\mathcal P$ divides both $x$ and $a$; this depends only on which primes of $\mathcal P$ divide $x$, i.e. only on $x\bmod L$. By the second form of (2), for $x\ge a_1$:
$$x\in\mathcal A\iff x+L\in\mathcal A .$$
So the elements of $\mathcal A$ that are $\ge a_1+L$ are exactly $a_1+L<a_2+L<a_3+L<\cdots$. Let $T\ge1$ be the number of elements of $\mathcal A$ below $a_1+L$ (they are $a_1,\dots,a_T$). Then the $(T+n)$-th element of $\mathcal A$ is the $n$-th element that is $\ge a_1+L$, i.e.
$$a_{n+T}=a_n+L\qquad\text{for all } n\ge1.$$
∎
